extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI, or assessment based on quality management system plus technical documentation review by a notified body under Annex VII.

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometric systems), the provider may choose internal control (Annex VI) or notified-body assessment (Annex VII), depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied.

For high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, providers generally follow the internal control procedure under Annex VI, with most such systems using self-assessment rather than notified body review.

Where a high-risk AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, Section A, the provider must follow the conformity assessment procedure required by that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies ensuring the AI-specific requirements are also assessed.

For the purposes of the conformity assessment procedure under Annex VII, the provider may choose any notified body, except that where the high-risk AI system is intended to be put into service by law enforcement, immigration, or asylum authorities or by Union institutions, the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body.
Substantial modifications to a high-risk AI system require a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in systems designed to continue learning after being placed on the market.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority, by way of derogation from Article 43, to authorise placing a specific high-risk AI system on the market without the normal conformity assessment for a limited period, for exceptional reasons such as public security, protection of life and health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets.

Annex VII grants notified bodies access to training and trained models, including relevant parameters, when necessary to assess conformity with Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, after other reasonable verification means have been exhausted.
Article 35 of the AI Act establishes the administrative framework for identification numbers and lists of notified bodies under the Act.

The Commission has proposed (COM(2025) 836 / 2025/0359 (COD)) a new Annex XIV listing codes, categories, and AI systems for the NANDO notified-body designation system, and corresponding amendments including to Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 for integration of AI Act high-risk requirements.

As of late June 2026, zero notified bodies had been designated under the Cyber Resilience Act (a separate regulation), illustrating general delays in EU notified-body designation processes, with a target of sufficient notified body capacity by 11 December 2026.
As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem specifically for the AI Act was still being built, with designation processes ongoing across member states and capacity limited.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act, including for medical device AI systems under MDR/IVDR interplay.

High-risk AI obligations under the AI Act are stated to fully apply from August 2026, after which notified bodies designated under the AI Act are expected to begin conducting AI Act-specific conformity assessments.
As of October 2025, the NANDO system listed 51 MDR-designated notified bodies and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies (medical devices regulations, not the AI Act specifically).

Providers must issue an EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) and affix CE marking (Article 48), referencing which conformity assessment procedure (Annex VI or Annex VII) was followed under Article 43.
The Commission may adopt delegated acts under Article 43(5) to update Annex VI and Annex VII in light of technical progress, without needing to revise the AI Act itself.

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures and Notified Body Designation Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes a two-track conformity assessment system for high-risk AI systems under Article 43, with most systems eligible for internal-control self-assessment and only a subset requiring notified-body review (medium-high confidence). However, the research indicates substantial uncertainty about the practical rollout: as of the most recent sources (early-to-mid 2026), no notified bodies appear to have been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, and the supporting administrative infrastructure (e.g., NANDO codes, Annex XIV) remains at the proposal stage (low confidence, but corroborated across several sources).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Routes
Article 43 sets out two main pathways for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI, or assessment via quality management system and technical documentation review by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment), [Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-compliance-checklist-high-risk-systems)).

For AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometric systems), providers may choose internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf), [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)).

For Annex III systems in points 2 to 8, providers generally use the internal control procedure under Annex VI, with self-assessment being the norm rather than notified-body review (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

Where a high-risk AI system is a safety component of a product under existing Union harmonisation legislation (Annex I, Section A), the sectoral conformity assessment procedure applies, with notified bodies also assessing AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

### Notified Body Selection and Access
Providers may generally choose any notified body for Annex VII assessments, except that for systems used by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions, the relevant market surveillance authority itself acts as the notified body (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Annex VII grants notified bodies access to training and trained models, including parameters, when necessary to verify compliance with Chapter III, Section 2 requirements (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

### Ongoing Obligations and Flexibility Mechanisms
Substantial modifications generally trigger a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously-learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to authorize market placement without standard conformity assessment, for a limited period, on exceptional grounds such as public security or health protection (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Providers must issue an EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) and affix CE marking (Article 48), referencing the assessment route used (low confidence) ([sota.io](https://sota.io/blog/eu-ai-act-eu-declaration-conformity-ce-marking-registration-saas-providers-2026)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
The Commission has proposed a new Annex XIV (COM(2025) 836) establishing NANDO codes and categories for AI Act notified-body designation, alongside amendments integrating AI Act requirements into aviation safety regulation (Regulation (EU) 2018/1139) — this remains a legislative proposal (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)). As of March–April 2026, sources indicate no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act itself (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act), [aiact-navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). By contrast, the adjacent Cyber Resilience Act had zero designated notified bodies as of June 2026 despite a December 2026 target, illustrating a broader pattern of designation delays (low confidence) ([cybercertlabs](https://www.cybercertlabs.com/case-studies/insights-cra-notified-bodies-2026)). For comparison, NANDO listed 51 MDR and 19 IVDR notified bodies as of October 2025 — figures for medical devices regulation, not the AI Act (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Two sources differ in emphasis regarding early-2026 designation status: one (March 2026) describes an active but incomplete designation process, while another (April 2026) states explicitly that zero formal AI Act designations existed — both agree no designations had occurred but differ in framing ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act) vs. [aiact-navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). Several claims about core Article 43 mechanics and Article 35 (notified body registry) carry low confidence (below 0.4), largely due to reliance on non-authoritative blog sources rather than the regulation text itself.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms whether any notified bodies have been designated under the AI Act as of October 2026. There is no definitive list of designated AI Act notified bodies or NANDO registration numbers. It remains unclear whether Annex XIV/COM(2025) 836 has been formally adopted. The interaction between sectoral (e.g., MDR/IVDR) and AI Act notified bodies for dual-regime products is unaddressed, as are the practical consequences for providers if no notified bodies exist by the August 2026 high-risk compliance deadline.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures and Notified Body Designation Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes a two-track conformity assessment system for high-risk AI systems under Article 43, with most systems eligible for internal-control self-assessment and only a subset requiring notified-body review (medium-high confidence). However, the research indicates substantial uncertainty about the practical rollout: as of the most recent sources (early-to-mid 2026), no notified bodies appear to have been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, and the supporting administrative infrastructure (e.g., NANDO codes, Annex XIV) remains at the proposal stage (low confidence, but corroborated across several sources).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Routes
Article 43 sets out two main pathways for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI, or assessment via quality management system and technical documentation review by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment), [Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-compliance-checklist-high-risk-systems)).

For AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometric systems), providers may choose internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf), [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)).

For Annex III systems in points 2 to 8, providers generally use the internal control procedure under Annex VI, with self-assessment being the norm rather than notified-body review (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

Where a high-risk AI system is a safety component of a product under existing Union harmonisation legislation (Annex I, Section A), the sectoral conformity assessment procedure applies, with notified bodies also assessing AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

### Notified Body Selection and Access
Providers may generally choose any notified body for Annex VII assessments, except that for systems used by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions, the relevant market surveillance authority itself acts as the notified body (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Annex VII grants notified bodies access to training and trained models, including parameters, when necessary to verify compliance with Chapter III, Section 2 requirements (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

### Ongoing Obligations and Flexibility Mechanisms
Substantial modifications generally trigger a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously-learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to authorize market placement without standard conformity assessment, for a limited period, on exceptional grounds such as public security or health protection (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Providers must issue an EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) and affix CE marking (Article 48), referencing the assessment route used (low confidence) ([sota.io](https://sota.io/blog/eu-ai-act-eu-declaration-conformity-ce-marking-registration-saas-providers-2026)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
The Commission has proposed a new Annex XIV (COM(2025) 836) establishing NANDO codes and categories for AI Act notified-body designation, alongside amendments integrating AI Act requirements into aviation safety regulation (Regulation (EU) 2018/1139) — this remains a legislative proposal (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)). As of March–April 2026, sources indicate no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act itself (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act), [aiact-navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). By contrast, the adjacent Cyber Resilience Act had zero designated notified bodies as of June 2026 despite a December 2026 target, illustrating a broader pattern of designation delays (low confidence) ([cybercertlabs](https://www.cybercertlabs.com/case-studies/insights-cra-notified-bodies-2026)). For comparison, NANDO listed 51 MDR and 19 IVDR notified bodies as of October 2025 — figures for medical devices regulation, not the AI Act (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Two sources differ in emphasis regarding early-2026 designation status: one (March 2026) describes an active but incomplete designation process, while another (April 2026) states explicitly that zero formal AI Act designations existed — both agree no designations had occurred but differ in framing ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act) vs. [aiact-navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). Several claims about core Article 43 mechanics and Article 35 (notified body registry) carry low confidence (below 0.4), largely due to reliance on non-authoritative blog sources rather than the regulation text itself.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms whether any notified bodies have been designated under the AI Act as of October 2026. There is no definitive list of designated AI Act notified bodies or NANDO registration numbers. It remains unclear whether Annex XIV/COM(2025) 836 has been formally adopted. The interaction between sectoral (e.g., MDR/IVDR) and AI Act notified bodies for dual-regime products is unaddressed, as are the practical consequences for providers if no notified bodies exist by the August 2026 high-risk compliance deadline.
